source.text: Τῇ δὲ δευτέρᾳ ὁράσει εἶδες αὐτὴν ἑστηκυῖαν καὶ τὴν ὄψιν νεωτέραν ἔχουσαν καὶ ἱλαρωτέραν παρὰ τὸ πρότερον, τὴν δὲ σάρκα καὶ τὰς τρίχας πρεσβυτέρας. ἄκουε, φησίν, καὶ ταύτην τὴν παραβολήν. 2. ὅταν πρεσβύτερός τις, ἤδη ἀφηλπικὼς ἑαυτὸν διὰ τὴν ἀσθένειαν αὐτοῦ καὶ τὴν πτωχότητα, οὐδὲν ἕτερον προσδέχεται εἰ μὴ τὴν ἐσχάτην ἡμέραν τῆς ζωῆς αὐτοῦ· εἶτα ἐξαίφνης κατελείφθη αὐτῷ κληρονομία, ἀκούσας δὲ ἐξηγέρθη καὶ περιχαρὴς γενόμενος ἐνεδύσατο τὴν ἰσχύν, καὶ οὐκέτι ἀνάκειται, ἀλλὰ ἕστηκεν, καὶ ἀνανεοῦται αὐτοῦ τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἤδη ἐφθαρμένον ἀπὸ τῶν προτέρων αὐτοῦ πράξεων, καὶ οὐκέτι κάθηται, ἀλλὰ ἀνδρίζεται· οὕτως καὶ ὑμεῖς, ἀκούσαντες τὴν ἀποκάλυψιν ἣν ὑμῖν ὁ Κύριος ἀπεκάλυψεν. 3. ὅτι ἐσπλαγχνίσθη ἐφ’ ὑμᾶς, καὶ ἀνενεώσατο τὰ πνεύματα ὑμῶν, καὶ ἀπέθεσθε τὰς μαλακίας ὑμῶν, καὶ προσῆλθεν ὑμῖν ἰσχυρότης καὶ ἐδυναμώθητε ἐν τῇ πίστει, καὶ ἰδὼν ὁ Κύριος τὴν ἰσχυροποίησιν ὑμῶν ἐχάρη· καὶ διὰ τοῦτο ἐδήλωσεν ὑμῖν τὴν οἰκοδομὴν τοῦ πύργου, καὶ ἕτερα δηλώσει, ἐὰν ἐξ ὅλης καρδίας εἰρηνεύετε ἐν ἑαυτοῖς.
source.label: Vision 3, section xii

translation.text:
But in the second vision you saw her standing, with a countenance[a] younger and more cheerful than before, though her flesh and her hair were older. “Listen,” she says, “to this parable also.

“When an old man, having already given up hope for himself because of his weakness and his poverty, expects nothing else but the last day of his life; then, all at once, an inheritance is left to him. On hearing of it he rises up, and, becoming overjoyed, he puts on strength; he no longer lies down, but stands; his spirit—already corrupted by his former deeds—is renewed; and he no longer sits, but takes courage[b]. So also you, when you heard the revelation that the Lord revealed to you.

“For he had compassion on you and renewed your spirits, and you put away your softness[c]; strength came to you and you were strengthened in faith[d]; and when the Lord saw your strengthening, he rejoiced. For this reason he made known to you the building of the tower[f], and he will make other things known, if, with a whole heart, you are at peace among yourselves[e].”

footnotes.text: “Countenance” translates ὄψις, which can mean face or appearance; the point is her visibly younger, more cheerful look.
“Takes courage” renders ἀνδρίζεται, literally “acts like a man,” an idiom for showing courage.
“Softness” (μαλακία) in ancient moral language denotes laxity or lack of resolve, not a gendered slur in this context. Alternatives: “weakness,” “cowardice.”
“In faith” could also be read “in the faith”; the Greek uses the article with an abstract noun.
“Be at peace among yourselves” renders εἰρηνεύετε ἐν ἑαυτοῖς, an idiom for mutual peace within the community.
The “building of the tower” refers back to the tower imagery earlier in this vision, where the tower symbolizes the community being built.

lexical_decisions.rationale: Conveys both facial look and demeanor; enables the contrast with “flesh” and “hair.”
Denotes glad, cheerful disposition; “cheerful” fits the moral tone of renewed hope.
Here literal bodily flesh is in view; preserving “flesh” maintains the concrete imagery.
Literal reference to the woman’s hair in the vision.
Hermas uses short illustrative comparisons; “parable” is established and accurate.
Context is age in a parable, not church office; “old man” avoids ecclesiastical sense.

lexical_decisions.chosen: having already given up hope for himself
lexical_decisions.rationale: Expresses total loss of hope; participial nuance kept in English.
General lack of strength suits the parable’s physical and moral tone.
Material poverty is the point of contrast with the sudden inheritance.
Idiomatic expression for the end of life; “last day of his life” clarifies scope.

lexical_decisions.chosen: an inheritance is left to him
alternatives: an inheritance is bequeathed to him
lexical_decisions.rationale: Legal-bequest sense is primary; passive renders the aorist passive nuance.
Vivid, active rendering fits the awakening of hope.
Intensifies joy upon hearing of the inheritance.
Preserves the clothing metaphor, common in biblical-Greek idiom.
In contrast with “stands”; “lies down” communicates inactivity.
Simple physical stance, marking renewed vigor.
Captures restoration after decay.
Human spirit (not the Holy Spirit) suits plural in v.3 and individual context.
Moral-spiritual deterioration from former deeds is in view.
Standard moral term matching Hermas’s usage.
Continues the posture contrast (lie/stand/sit).
Idiomatic sense is moral courage; we avoid gendered phrasing while noting literal sense.
Established term for divine disclosure.
Divine referent; matches Cartha policy to render as “Lord.”
Denotes deep mercy; either alternative is accurate; “had compassion” is chosen for dignity.
Divine subject renews the people’s spirits.
Common moral metaphor for renouncing a vice or disposition.
Hermas’s moral “softness” (lack of resolve); we keep the vivid metaphor and explain in a note.
Abstract noun; personified arrival of strength fits the rhetoric.
Passive/middle nuance preserved; divine agency implied by context.
Here the interior disposition of trust is prominent; article with abstract is customary.
Nominal form keeps the parallel with “strength.”
Simple, fitting divine joy at their strengthening.
Different verb from ἀποκαλύπτω; “made known” preserves lexical distinction.
Concrete act of building the tower is intended, not metaphorical “edification” in English here.
Fixed image in Hermas for the church; we retain the concrete noun.
Keeps verbal parallel with ἐδήλωσεν in previous clause.

alternatives: live in peace with one another
lexical_decisions.rationale: Idiomatic plural reflexive points to mutual peace within the community.
Hebraic idiom preserved; “with a whole heart” keeps solemn register.

theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Render κύριος as “the Lord,” referring to God’s agency in revealing and rejoicing.
theological_decisions.rationale: Context assigns divine initiative and joy; Cartha policy translates κύριος as “Lord” for divine referent.

theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Translate as “faith” (interior trust) rather than a technical sense “the faith.”
theological_decisions.rationale: The collocation “were strengthened in faith” emphasizes their renewed trusting disposition after God’s compassion.

theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Human spirits, not the Holy Spirit.
theological_decisions.rationale: Plural “your spirits” (v.3) and individual context in v.2 indicate human interior life rather than the Spirit.

theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Communal peace (“among yourselves”) as the condition for further revelation.
theological_decisions.rationale: Plural imperative with reflexive pronoun in reciprocal sense points to mutual peace in the community.

theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Retain “softness” to preserve Hermas’s moral imagery of laxity/lack of resolve.
theological_decisions.rationale: Hermas contrasts softness with strength in faith; we keep the metaphor and explain in a note to avoid anachronistic gender connotations.

theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Translate literally as “the building of the tower,” preserving the symbolic image of the church.
theological_decisions.rationale: Hermas’s vision uses a concrete tower as allegory for the community; literal rendering keeps the apocalyptic texture.

review_passes.summary: The draft is excellent and captures the vivid, parabolic register of Hermas well. Two minor corrections were made: restoring the causal conjunction ὅτι ('For') at the beginning of verse 3, which connects the Lord's compassion to the renewal of their spirits, and inserting the missing footnote marker [a] into the text.
issues_found: Omission of the causal conjunction ὅτι at the beginning of verse 3. Adding 'For' restores the logical connection.
Footnote marker [a] was defined in the metadata but missing from the main text.

translation.text: “Picture an old man who has lost all hope because he is weak and poor. He expects nothing but the final day of his life. Then suddenly he learns that an inheritance has been left to him. The news stirs him, and joy fills him. He is clothed with strength. He no longer lies down, but stands up. His spirit, which his former deeds had already corrupted, is renewed. He no longer sits still, but takes courage. The same thing happened to you when you heard the revelation the Lord gave you.”

simplification_decisions.pob_phrase: When an old man, having already given up hope for himself because of his weakness and his poverty, expects nothing else but the last day of his life
simplification_decisions.simplified_phrase: Picture an old man who has lost all hope because he is weak and poor. He expects nothing but the final day of his life.
simplification_decisions.preserved_meaning: Weakness and poverty have left the man without hope, expecting only death.
simplification_decisions.reasoning_layer_used: POB main text and immediate comparison
simplification_decisions.rationale: Two direct sentences replace the dense opening clause while retaining its causes and force.

simplification_decisions.pob_phrase: On hearing of it he is stirred up, and, becoming overjoyed, he puts on strength
simplification_decisions.simplified_phrase: The news stirs him, and joy fills him. He is clothed with strength.
simplification_decisions.preserved_meaning: News of the inheritance fills him with joy and restores his vigor.
simplification_decisions.rationale: The sequence is clarified while the clothing image for strength is preserved without adding “new.”

simplification_decisions.pob_phrase: So also you, when you heard the revelation that the Lord revealed to you
simplification_decisions.simplified_phrase: The same thing happened to you when you heard the revelation the Lord gave you.
simplification_decisions.preserved_meaning: The Lord’s revelation affected the addressee as the inheritance affected the old man.
simplification_decisions.reasoning_layer_used: POB main text and analogy structure
simplification_decisions.rationale: The compressed comparison becomes a complete English sentence without changing its point.

interpretive_expansions.pob_phrase: So also you, when you heard the revelation that the Lord revealed to you
interpretive_expansions.rendering: The same thing happened to you when you heard the revelation the Lord gave you.
interpretive_expansions.claim: The addressee experienced the renewal illustrated by the old man.
evidence: The words “So also you” directly apply the preceding comparison to the addressee.
The immediate context describes the old man’s revival after hearing good news.
alternatives_preserved: The comparison may encompass the whole preceding sequence rather than one specific effect.

risk_flags.risk: “The same thing happened to you” states the comparison’s implied result explicitly.
risk_flags.mitigation: The immediate analogy supplies the result, and the wording does not define it more narrowly.

spob_revision_history.previous_text: “Picture an old man who has lost all hope because he is weak and poor. He expects nothing but the final day of his life. Then suddenly he learns that someone has left him an inheritance. The news stirs him, and joy fills him. He is clothed with new strength. He no longer lies down, but stands up. His spirit, which his former deeds had already corrupted, is renewed. He no longer sits still, but takes courage. The same thing happened to you when you heard the revelation the Lord gave you.”
spob_revision_history.review_summary: This is substantially clearer than POB and rightly makes the analogy’s implied outcome into a complete modern sentence; the immediate comparison supports that clarification without imposing doctrine. Revise two small additions: retain the passive statement that an inheritance was left to him, and do not add “new” to strength. The remaining modernization preserves the sequence, contrast, corruption/renewal imagery, and intended comparison.

base_translation.text: “For he had compassion on you and renewed your spirits, and you put away your softness; strength came to you and you were strengthened in faith; and when the Lord saw your strengthening, he rejoiced. For this reason he made known to you the building of the tower, and he will make other things known, if, with a whole heart, you are at peace among yourselves.”

translation.text: For he had compassion on you and renewed your spirits. You cast aside your weakness, and strength came to you. You grew strong in faith, and when the Lord saw this, he rejoiced. That is why he showed you the tower being built. He will also reveal other things to you if you live at peace with one another wholeheartedly.

simplification_decisions.preserved_meaning: They abandoned the lack of resolve that had left them spiritually weak.
simplification_decisions.rationale: “Weakness” makes the moral and spiritual sense of “softness” clear without sounding physical or childish.

simplification_decisions.pob_phrase: strength came to you and you were strengthened in faith
simplification_decisions.simplified_phrase: strength came to you. You grew strong in faith
simplification_decisions.preserved_meaning: They received strength and became firmer in faith.
simplification_decisions.rationale: Two short clauses preserve both the coming of strength and its effect on their faith.

simplification_decisions.preserved_meaning: The Lord revealed the ongoing construction of the tower.
simplification_decisions.rationale: The active wording is easier to picture while retaining the tower-building image.

risk_flags.risk: “Weakness” may cover a broader range than POB’s “softness.”
risk_flags.mitigation: The surrounding references to strength and stronger faith keep the intended contrast clear.

risk_flags.risk: “Live at peace” states the condition more naturally than “are at peace.”
risk_flags.mitigation: “With one another wholeheartedly” preserves both the communal and whole-heart requirements.
